questions.unit: Unit 1: Exploring One-Variable Data and Collecting Data
questions.prompt: A dataset of 10 observations has mean 20. One observation, 29, is removed. What is the mean of the remaining 9 observations?
questions.explanation: The original total is 10(20) = 200. After removing 29, the remaining total is 171, so the new mean is 171/9 = 19.0.

questions.unit: Unit 3: Inference for Categorical Data: Proportions
questions.prompt: A city survey estimates that between 62% and 70% of all households use a municipal service, at 95% confidence. Which public report is statistically appropriate?

choices.A: The true percentage changes from 62% to 70% in 95% of years.
choices.B: Exactly 95% of sampled households have usage rates between 62% and 70%.
choices.C: Based on the sampling method, 62% to 70% is a plausible range for the percentage of all city households using the service.
choices.D: There is a 95% chance that every nonsampled household uses the service.

questions.correctAnswerText: Based on the sampling method, 62% to 70% is a plausible range for the percentage of all city households using the service.
questions.explanation: The interval estimates one fixed citywide proportion using a method with a stated repeated-sampling confidence rate. It does not describe a time-varying parameter or the certainty of individual household behavior.

questions.unit: Unit 2: Probability, Random Variables, and Probability Distributions
questions.prompt: A fair eight-sided die is labeled 1 through 8. Given that the result is greater than 3, what is the probability that it is even?
questions.explanation: Given a result greater than 3, the possible outcomes are 4, 5, 6, 7, and 8. Three of those five outcomes—4, 6, and 8—are even, so the conditional probability is 3/5.

questions.unit: Unit 4: Inference for Quantitative Data: Means
questions.prompt: Two laboratories will compare mean readings from two measurement methods. Which design most effectively removes specimen-to-specimen variation from the method comparison?

choices.A: Use different convenient specimens in the two laboratories.
choices.B: Let each laboratory choose specimens expected to favor its method.
choices.C: Apply both methods to each randomly selected specimen, randomizing method order when order could matter.
choices.D: Compare one measurement from each method without recording the specimen.

questions.correctAnswerText: Apply both methods to each randomly selected specimen, randomizing method order when order could matter.
questions.explanation: Using both methods on each specimen creates paired data and removes between-specimen variation from the method comparison. Randomizing order limits order effects.

questions.unit: Unit 5: Regression Analysis
questions.prompt: A marine biologist wants to use water temperature to predict the number of feeding visits at individual tide-pool observation sessions. Which question most clearly defines the intended regression analysis and its observational unit?

choices.A: What is the mean water temperature across all sessions, ignoring feeding visits?
choices.B: Do warm sessions and cool sessions receive the same categorical label?
choices.C: How many feeding visits occurred at all tide pools combined?
choices.D: How does the number of feeding visits per session tend to change with water temperature measured during that same session?

questions.correctAnswerText: How does the number of feeding visits per session tend to change with water temperature measured during that same session?
questions.explanation: The question identifies two quantitative variables measured on the same observational unit, a tide-pool session, and makes temperature the explanatory variable used to predict the session's feeding-visit count.

questions.unit: Unit 1: Exploring One-Variable Data and Collecting Data
questions.prompt: A survey contains two policy questions, and researchers are concerned that the first question may influence answers to the second. Which design best assesses a question-order effect?

choices.A: Ask interviewers which order they believe is less biased.
choices.B: Give every respondent order AB so administration is consistent.
choices.C: Let respondents choose the question they answer first.
choices.D: Randomly assign respondents to receive the questions in order AB or BA and compare responses.

questions.correctAnswerText: Randomly assign respondents to receive the questions in order AB or BA and compare responses.
questions.explanation: Random assignment makes the order groups comparable, so systematic response differences can be attributed to question order for the respondents studied.

questions.unit: Unit 3: Inference for Categorical Data: Proportions
questions.prompt: A 95% confidence interval for the population proportion p of users who enable a feature is (0.62, 0.70). Let q = 1 − p be the population proportion who do not enable it. What is the corresponding 95% confidence interval for q?
questions.explanation: The transformation q = 1 − p reverses the interval endpoints. The lower endpoint is 1 − 0.70 = 0.30 and the upper endpoint is 1 − 0.62 = 0.38; the confidence level remains 95%.

questions.unit: Unit 2: Probability, Random Variables, and Probability Distributions
questions.prompt: A random variable X has variance 0. Which statement must be true?

choices.A: X is normally distributed.
choices.B: X equals one constant value with probability 1.
choices.C: X has mean 0.
choices.D: X takes positive and negative values with equal probability.

questions.correctAnswerText: X equals one constant value with probability 1.
questions.explanation: Variance is the expected squared distance from the mean. It can be zero only when that distance is zero with probability 1, so X is constant at its mean.

questions.unit: Unit 4: Inference for Quantitative Data: Means
questions.prompt: A researcher tests H0: μ_X = 40 against Ha: μ_X > 40 and obtains t = 2.10. The variable is redefined as Y = 100 − X. Which statement gives the equivalent test using Y?

choices.A: H0: μ_Y = 40 against Ha: μ_Y > 40, with t = 2.10
choices.B: H0: μ_Y = 60 against Ha: μ_Y > 60, with t = −2.10
choices.C: H0: μ_Y = 60 against Ha: μ_Y < 60, with t = −2.10 and the same one-sided p-value
choices.D: H0: μ_Y = 60 against Ha: μ_Y < 60, with t = 2.10 and a different p-value

questions.correctAnswerText: H0: μ_Y = 60 against Ha: μ_Y < 60, with t = −2.10 and the same one-sided p-value
questions.explanation: The transformation reverses direction: μ_X = 40 corresponds to μ_Y = 60, and μ_X > 40 corresponds to μ_Y < 60. Multiplication by −1 reverses the sign of t, while the equivalent lower-tail area equals the original upper-tail p-value.

questions.unit: Unit 1: Exploring One-Variable Data and Collecting Data
questions.prompt: A histogram displays exact frequencies for intervals but not the individual observations within each interval. Which quantity can always be determined exactly from the histogram?

choices.A: The sample standard deviation
choices.B: The sample mean
choices.C: The sample median
choices.D: The total number of observations

questions.correctAnswerText: The total number of observations
questions.explanation: Exact bar frequencies can be summed to obtain n. Without the individual positions inside bins, the exact mean, median, and standard deviation generally cannot be recovered.

questions.unit: Unit 5: Regression Analysis
questions.prompt: Four residuals from a fitted regression line are −2, 1, 0, and 3. What is the sum of squared residuals for these four observations?
questions.explanation: SSE is the sum of squared residuals: (−2)² + 1² + 0² + 3² = 4 + 1 + 0 + 9 = 14.

questions.unit: Unit 3: Inference for Categorical Data: Proportions
questions.prompt: A researcher wants to estimate how the population proportion using automatic payment differs between customers under age 30 and customers age 30 or older. Which parameter matches the goal?

choices.A: p_under30 − p_30plus
choices.B: p̂_under30 − p̂_30plus
choices.C: μ_under30 − μ_30plus
choices.D: The number of sampled customers using automatic payment

questions.correctAnswerText: p_under30 − p_30plus
questions.explanation: The target is a difference between two population proportions. The corresponding sample proportions are statistics used to estimate this parameter.

questions.unit: Unit 2: Probability, Random Variables, and Probability Distributions
questions.prompt: A theater row has 20 labeled seats, and four friends will receive four distinct seats at random. Which simulation plan best estimates the probability that no two friends receive adjacent seats?

choices.A: Generate four integers from 1 to 20 with replacement and count trials with no consecutive values.
choices.B: Choose one set of four nonadjacent seats and repeat that same assignment many times.
choices.C: Generate the number of adjacent seat pairs directly from a normal distribution.
choices.D: Randomly select four distinct seat numbers without replacement, record whether none are consecutive, and repeat for many trials.

questions.correctAnswerText: Randomly select four distinct seat numbers without replacement, record whether none are consecutive, and repeat for many trials.
questions.explanation: Each trial must reproduce four distinct random seat assignments. Recording the no-consecutive-seats indicator and repeating many times makes its relative frequency an estimate of the desired probability.

questions.unit: Unit 1: Exploring One-Variable Data and Collecting Data
questions.prompt: The modal response category in a survey contains 35% of responses. Which statement is correct?

choices.A: The category contains a majority because it is the mode.
choices.B: The category must also contain the median response.
choices.C: It is the most common category, but it does not contain a majority of responses.
choices.D: The remaining categories must each contain exactly 65% of responses.

questions.correctAnswerText: It is the most common category, but it does not contain a majority of responses.
questions.explanation: A mode is the category with the greatest frequency. A majority requires more than 50%, and 35% is not a majority.

questions.unit: Unit 4: Inference for Quantitative Data: Means
questions.prompt: For a t distribution with df = 12, the upper-tail areas beyond t = 2.179 and t = 3.055 are 0.025 and 0.005, respectively. A two-sided test produces |t| = 2.50. Which range contains the p-value?

choices.A: Greater than 0.10
choices.B: Between 0.005 and 0.025
choices.C: Between 0.05 and 0.10
choices.D: Between 0.01 and 0.05

questions.correctAnswerText: Between 0.01 and 0.05
questions.explanation: Because 2.179 < 2.50 < 3.055, one upper-tail area is between 0.005 and 0.025. A two-sided p-value doubles that area, placing it between 0.01 and 0.05.

questions.unit: Unit 3: Inference for Categorical Data: Proportions
questions.prompt: A one-proportion test of H0: p = 0.40 against Ha: p > 0.40 has α = 0.05 and power 0.80 when p = 0.50. Which pair of probabilities is correct?

choices.A: P(reject H0 | p = 0.40) = 0.95 and P(fail to reject H0 | p = 0.50) = 0.80
choices.B: P(reject H0 | p = 0.40) = 0.20 and P(fail to reject H0 | p = 0.50) = 0.05
choices.C: P(reject H0 | p = 0.40) = 0.05 and P(fail to reject H0 | p = 0.50) = 0.20
choices.D: P(reject H0 | p = 0.40) = 0.80 and P(fail to reject H0 | p = 0.50) = 0.95

questions.correctAnswerText: P(reject H0 | p = 0.40) = 0.05 and P(fail to reject H0 | p = 0.50) = 0.20
questions.explanation: The significance level is the rejection probability when the null value is true, so the first probability is 0.05. Power is 0.80 at p = 0.50, so the Type II probability there is 1 − 0.80 = 0.20.

questions.unit: Unit 1: Exploring One-Variable Data and Collecting Data
questions.prompt: A skating association wants to describe variation in lap times for all competitors at a national event. Which parameter most directly matches that goal?

choices.A: The sample mean lap time among competitors timed by one volunteer
choices.B: The population median rank of the competitors
choices.C: The population standard deviation of competitors' lap times
choices.D: The proportion of sampled competitors with lap times below their sample mean

questions.correctAnswerText: The population standard deviation of competitors' lap times
questions.explanation: The target is variability in one quantitative variable for the full population of competitors. The population standard deviation, σ, directly describes that spread; a sample mean and a proportion target different features.

questions.unit: Unit 2: Probability, Random Variables, and Probability Distributions
questions.stimulus: The fill error X, in grams, for a packaging machine is normally distributed with mean 0.4 gram and standard deviation 1.2 grams. Errors on independently selected packages are independent. Use Φ(1.00) = 0.8413, Φ(3.00) = 0.99865, and the 10th-percentile standard normal value z = −1.282.
questions.prompt: For X normally distributed with mean 0.4 gram and standard deviation 1.2 grams, what is P(X > 1.6 grams) for one randomly selected package?

questions.unit: Unit 2: Probability, Random Variables, and Probability Distributions
questions.stimulus: The fill error X, in grams, for a packaging machine is normally distributed with mean 0.4 gram and standard deviation 1.2 grams. Errors on independently selected packages are independent. Use Φ(1.00) = 0.8413, Φ(3.00) = 0.99865, and the 10th-percentile standard normal value z = −1.282.
questions.prompt: For a normal fill-error distribution with mean 0.4 gram and standard deviation 1.2 grams, what is the 10th percentile, approximately? Use z = −1.282.

choices.A: −1.14 grams
choices.B: −0.88 gram
choices.C: 0.12 gram
choices.D: 1.94 grams

questions.correctAnswerText: −1.14 grams
questions.explanation: Convert the supplied 10th-percentile z-value to the original scale: x = 0.4 + (−1.282)(1.2) = −1.1384 grams, approximately −1.14 grams.

questions.unit: Unit 2: Probability, Random Variables, and Probability Distributions
questions.stimulus: The fill error X, in grams, for a packaging machine is normally distributed with mean 0.4 gram and standard deviation 1.2 grams. Errors on independently selected packages are independent. Use Φ(1.00) = 0.8413, Φ(3.00) = 0.99865, and the 10th-percentile standard normal value z = −1.282.
questions.prompt: For a random sample of 9 packages, x̄ is normally distributed with mean 0.4 gram and standard deviation 1.2/√9 = 0.4 gram. What is P(x̄ > 1.6 grams), and what does it describe?

choices.A: 0.1587, the chance that one package exceeds 1.6 grams
choices.B: 0.00135, the chance that the average error of 9 packages exceeds 1.6 grams
choices.C: 0.0228, the chance that all 9 packages exceed 1.6 grams
choices.D: 0.99865, the chance that the average error is below its mean

questions.correctAnswerText: 0.00135, the chance that the average error of 9 packages exceeds 1.6 grams
questions.explanation: The standardized sample mean is z = (1.6 − 0.4)/0.4 = 3.00. Thus P(x̄ > 1.6) = 1 − 0.99865 = 0.00135, a probability about the nine-package average rather than one package.

questions.unit: Unit 5: Regression Analysis
questions.prompt: Changing measurement units makes a fitted line's positive slope numerically large, while its correlation remains r = 0.20. What should be concluded?

choices.A: The linear association became strong when the slope's numerical value increased.
choices.B: The relationship became negative because r is below 1.
choices.C: The predicted response rises with x, but the standardized linear association remains weak.
choices.D: A large positive slope and r = 0.20 are mathematically incompatible.

questions.correctAnswerText: The predicted response rises with x, but the standardized linear association remains weak.
questions.explanation: The positive slope gives the direction of prediction, while r = 0.20 indicates weak linear association. Changing units can change the numerical slope but not the correlation.

questions.unit: Unit 3: Inference for Categorical Data: Proportions
questions.prompt: A website compares response proportions for two invitation messages. Which design best supports a causal comparison?

choices.A: Randomly assign eligible users to receive message A or B, then compare response proportions.
choices.B: Let users select which message they prefer to receive.
choices.C: Send A to new users and B to returning users.
choices.D: Send message A in the morning and message B in the evening.

questions.correctAnswerText: Randomly assign eligible users to receive message A or B, then compare response proportions.
questions.explanation: Random assignment balances other user characteristics across messages and supports a causal comparison of response proportions for eligible users in the experiment.

questions.unit: Unit 1: Exploring One-Variable Data and Collecting Data
questions.prompt: The dataset 2, 4, 6 has sample standard deviation 2. Each observation is then duplicated once, producing 2, 2, 4, 4, 6, 6. What is the sample standard deviation of the duplicated dataset, approximately?
questions.explanation: The duplicated values still have mean 4, and their squared deviations sum to 16. The sample variance is 16/(6 − 1) = 3.2, so the sample standard deviation is √3.2 ≈ 1.79; duplicating values changes the n − 1 divisor.

questions.unit: Unit 4: Inference for Quantitative Data: Means
questions.prompt: A random sample of households is measured before and after attic insulation is installed. Researchers want to estimate the population mean decrease in monthly energy use. Which procedure is appropriate?

choices.A: A one-sample t-interval for the within-household before-minus-after differences
choices.B: A two-sample t-interval treating before and after measurements as independent
choices.C: A one-proportion z-interval for households whose use decreases
choices.D: A one-sample t-interval using only the after-insulation measurements

questions.correctAnswerText: A one-sample t-interval for the within-household before-minus-after differences
questions.explanation: Before and after measurements come from the same household, so one quantitative difference is calculated per household and analyzed with a one-sample t procedure.

questions.unit: Unit 2: Probability, Random Variables, and Probability Distributions
questions.prompt: For a discrete random variable X, E(X) = 3 and E(X²) = 11. Using Var(X) = E(X²) − [E(X)]², what is the standard deviation of X?
questions.explanation: Var(X) = 11 − 3² = 2. Standard deviation is the nonnegative square root of variance, so σ_X = √2.

questions.unit: Unit 3: Inference for Categorical Data: Proportions
questions.prompt: A quality team tests H0: p = 0.02 after every additional 10 inspected items and stops the first time the p-value is below 0.05. It reports the final test as having α = 0.05. What is the main problem with that claim?

choices.A: A proportion can be tested only after every item in the population is inspected.
choices.B: The p-value must equal the observed sample proportion.
choices.C: Stopping early always increases the estimated defect proportion to 1.
choices.D: Repeatedly looking and stopping after a small p-value can make the overall Type I error probability exceed 0.05.

questions.correctAnswerText: Repeatedly looking and stopping after a small p-value can make the overall Type I error probability exceed 0.05.
questions.explanation: The 0.05 level applies to one prespecified analysis under its stated sampling plan. Repeated opportunities to stop on a rare small p-value increase the chance of at least one false rejection unless the procedure adjusts for sequential monitoring.

questions.unit: Unit 1: Exploring One-Variable Data and Collecting Data
questions.prompt: A software study compares two navigation layouts, and prior experience suggests that operating system strongly affects task time. Which design best controls this source of variation?

choices.A: Block participants by operating system, then randomly assign the two layouts within each block.
choices.B: Give one layout to all users of one operating system and the other layout to all remaining users.
choices.C: Allow each participant to choose the layout that appears easier.
choices.D: Ignore operating system and assign layouts in order of arrival without randomization.

questions.correctAnswerText: Block participants by operating system, then randomly assign the two layouts within each block.
questions.explanation: Blocking compares layouts among participants sharing the important operating-system characteristic. Random assignment within blocks prevents layout from being confounded with operating system and supports a causal comparison.

questions.unit: Unit 4: Inference for Quantitative Data: Means
questions.prompt: An analyst defines paired differences as d = after − before and obtains t = −2.40 with a two-sided p-value of 0.024 for H0: μ_d = 0. If the differences are instead defined as d′ = before − after, what result is obtained?

choices.A: t = −2.40 and p-value = 0.976
choices.B: t = 2.40 and p-value = 0.048
choices.C: t = 2.40 and p-value = 0.024
choices.D: t = 0 and p-value = 1

questions.correctAnswerText: t = 2.40 and p-value = 0.024
questions.explanation: Reversing every paired difference multiplies the sample mean difference and t statistic by −1. It does not change |t|, so a two-sided p-value remains 0.024.

questions.unit: Unit 4: Inference for Quantitative Data: Means
questions.prompt: A study samples 10 students from each of 6 randomly selected class sections and compares a quantitative outcome between two programs. The analysis treats all 60 students as independent. Which assessment is most appropriate?

choices.A: The analysis is valid because 60 is greater than 30.
choices.B: The analysis overstates uncertainty because students in a section must have negative correlation.
choices.C: The analysis may understate the standard error because outcomes of students in the same section can be positively associated.
choices.D: The analysis becomes a paired t procedure because each section contributes 10 students.

questions.correctAnswerText: The analysis may understate the standard error because outcomes of students in the same section can be positively associated.
questions.explanation: Students sampled from the same class section form clusters and need not provide independent information. Ignoring positive within-section association treats the effective amount of information as too large and can make the standard error too small.

questions.unit: Unit 1: Exploring One-Variable Data and Collecting Data
questions.prompt: A value of 72 has z-score 1.50 in a distribution with mean 60. What is the distribution's standard deviation?
questions.explanation: Use z = (x − μ)/σ. Substituting gives 1.50 = (72 − 60)/σ = 12/σ, so σ = 12/1.50 = 8.

questions.unit: Unit 2: Probability, Random Variables, and Probability Distributions
questions.prompt: Software repeatedly generates batches of 10 observations from a specified population model. To approximate the sampling distribution of x̄ for n = 10, which output from each batch should be saved?

choices.A: Its maximum observation
choices.B: Its arithmetic average
choices.C: The sign of its first observation
choices.D: The fixed population mean

questions.correctAnswerText: Its arithmetic average
questions.explanation: Each generated batch represents one sample of size 10, so saving its average produces one realization of x̄. Repeating this builds an approximation to the sampling distribution.

questions.unit: Unit 3: Inference for Categorical Data: Proportions
questions.prompt: A survey uses a probability sample, but some respondents systematically underreport a behavior. Which statement about a conventional confidence interval for the behavior's proportion is correct?

choices.A: The margin of error describes random sampling variability but does not account for systematic measurement bias.
choices.B: The confidence level automatically corrects inaccurate answers.
choices.C: Increasing confidence eliminates the underreporting.
choices.D: The interval is unbiased because the original sample was random.

questions.correctAnswerText: The margin of error describes random sampling variability but does not account for systematic measurement bias.
questions.explanation: Probability sampling supports the sampling-error calculation, but consistently inaccurate self-reports can shift the estimate and interval away from the true population proportion.

questions.unit: Unit 1: Exploring One-Variable Data and Collecting Data
questions.prompt: A new observation is added to a dataset, and the new value lies strictly between the old minimum and maximum. Which measure must remain unchanged?

choices.A: The mean
choices.B: The median
choices.C: The standard deviation
choices.D: The range

questions.correctAnswerText: The range
questions.explanation: A value strictly inside the old minimum and maximum changes neither endpoint, so the range remains unchanged. The mean, median, and standard deviation can change.

questions.unit: Unit 4: Inference for Quantitative Data: Means
questions.prompt: A sample of 16 observations consists entirely of the value 54. What happens when the usual one-sample t statistic is computed for testing H0: μ = 50?

choices.A: t = 0 because there is no sample variation.
choices.B: t = 1 because the sample has only one distinct value.
choices.C: t = 16 because every observation exceeds 50.
choices.D: No finite t statistic is produced because s = 0 makes the estimated standard error 0.

questions.correctAnswerText: No finite t statistic is produced because s = 0 makes the estimated standard error 0.
questions.explanation: With all observations equal, s = 0 and s/√n = 0. The numerator 54 − 50 is nonzero, so the usual t ratio requires division by zero and is not a finite statistic; the standard t procedure is inappropriate.

questions.unit: Unit 5: Regression Analysis
questions.stimulus: A least-squares regression predicts weekly output y from training hours x. The slope is positive. For the response values, the total sum of squares is SST = 250, and the regression sum of squared residuals is SSE = 90.
questions.prompt: For a regression with SST = 250 and SSE = 90, what is r²?

questions.unit: Unit 5: Regression Analysis
questions.stimulus: A least-squares regression predicts weekly output y from training hours x. The slope is positive. For the response values, the total sum of squares is SST = 250, and the regression sum of squared residuals is SSE = 90.
questions.prompt: For the regression with SST = 250, SSE = 90, and r² = 0.64, suppose 10 units are added to every weekly output y while the training-hour values remain unchanged. What happens to SST, SSE, and r²?

choices.A: SST increases, SSE stays fixed, and r² increases.
choices.B: SST and SSE remain unchanged, so r² remains 0.64.
choices.C: SST and SSE each increase by 10, so r² becomes 0.80.
choices.D: SST stays fixed, SSE decreases, and r² becomes 1.

questions.correctAnswerText: SST and SSE remain unchanged, so r² remains 0.64.
questions.explanation: Adding a constant to every response shifts both observed and fitted values equally. Deviations from ȳ and residuals are unchanged, so SST, SSE, and their ratio—and therefore r²—remain unchanged.

questions.unit: Unit 5: Regression Analysis
questions.stimulus: A least-squares regression predicts weekly output y from training hours x. The slope is positive. For the response values, the total sum of squares is SST = 250, and the regression sum of squared residuals is SSE = 90.
questions.prompt: For a regression with SST = 250 and SSE = 90, which interpretation is correct?

choices.A: The line predicts every weekly output within 36% of its observed value.
choices.B: Training hours cause exactly 64% of each worker's output.
choices.C: The line accounts for 64% of the variation in weekly output, while 36% remains in squared residual variation.
choices.D: The correlation equals SSE/SST = 0.36.

questions.correctAnswerText: The line accounts for 64% of the variation in weekly output, while 36% remains in squared residual variation.
questions.explanation: The unexplained fraction is SSE/SST = 90/250 = 0.36, so the explained fraction is 1 − 0.36 = 0.64. This describes variation, not individual causal percentages.

questions.unit: Unit 2: Probability, Random Variables, and Probability Distributions
questions.prompt: For a Bernoulli random variable with success probability p, the variance is p(1 − p). At which value of p is this variance largest?
questions.explanation: The product p(1 − p) is symmetric around 0.50 and reaches its maximum value 0.25 at p = 0.50.

questions.unit: Unit 3: Inference for Categorical Data: Proportions
questions.prompt: A one-proportion test produces z = 2.05 for Ha: p > p0. The standard normal upper-tail probability beyond 2.05 is 0.020. What is the p-value?
questions.explanation: Because Ha is right-tailed, the p-value is the upper-tail probability beyond the observed positive z statistic. The supplied area is 0.020 and is not doubled.

questions.unit: Unit 3: Inference for Categorical Data: Proportions
questions.prompt: Researchers conduct 20 unrelated tests whose null hypotheses are all true, each at α = 0.05, and publicize only the smallest p-value. Which concern is most appropriate?

choices.A: Every test must have a p-value greater than 0.05 because all null hypotheses are true.
choices.B: Searching across many tests makes at least one false positive more likely than the 0.05 rate for a single prespecified test.
choices.C: The smallest p-value is the probability that all 20 null hypotheses are true.
choices.D: Publishing one result changes the sample proportion in every other test.

questions.correctAnswerText: Searching across many tests makes at least one false positive more likely than the 0.05 rate for a single prespecified test.
questions.explanation: Each true-null test has a 0.05 false-positive probability, but selecting the smallest result from many tests creates multiple opportunities for a false rejection. The highlighted p-value does not account for that search.

questions.unit: Unit 1: Exploring One-Variable Data and Collecting Data
questions.prompt: A telephone survey uses multiple interviewers. Which step best reduces interviewer effects?

choices.A: Allow each interviewer to paraphrase questions freely.
choices.B: Assign each interviewer to only one demographic group.
choices.C: Train interviewers to use the same neutral script and monitor adherence to the protocol.
choices.D: Tell interviewers the responses the sponsor expects.

questions.correctAnswerText: Train interviewers to use the same neutral script and monitor adherence to the protocol.
questions.explanation: Standardized neutral wording and monitoring reduce systematic differences caused by interviewer delivery or expectations.

questions.unit: Unit 1: Exploring One-Variable Data and Collecting Data
questions.prompt: A beverage company wants to compare taste ratings for two labels placed on the same drink. Which design best isolates the label effect?

choices.A: Randomly assign coded labels to otherwise identical drink samples and blind tasters to the study hypothesis.
choices.B: Put label A on one flavor and label B on a different flavor.
choices.C: Let tasters choose which label they receive.
choices.D: Compare current customers shown label A with last year's customers shown label B.

questions.correctAnswerText: Randomly assign coded labels to otherwise identical drink samples and blind tasters to the study hypothesis.
questions.explanation: Keeping the drink identical isolates label as the treatment, random assignment creates comparable groups, and blinding reduces expectation effects.
